claims.text: Local lattice distortion caused by atomic size misfit is the principal factor governing hardness in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortion caused by atomic size misfit is the principal factor governing strength in single-phase high-entropy alloys.
Atomic size misfit produces local lattice distortion.
Local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Substitution with elements having different atomic radii can systematically increase or decrease atomic size mismatch.
Processing conditions and grain size should be held as similar as possible while atomic size mismatch is varied.
The comparison requires the alloys to remain single-phase solid solutions without precipitation or significant segregation.
X-ray diffraction line broadening or microscopy-based local strain mapping can reveal atomic-scale lattice distortion.
Greater atomic size mismatch increases local lattice distortion.
Greater lattice distortion hinders dislocation movement.
Hindered dislocation movement elevates yield strength.
Reducing atomic size misfit should reduce lattice strain and lower hardness and strength.
Single-phase alloys with increased atomic size mismatch will have greater hardness than the baseline alloy.
Single-phase alloys with increased atomic size mismatch will have greater strength than the baseline alloy.
Single-phase alloys with reduced atomic size mismatch will have lower hardness and strength than the baseline alloy.
The proposed relationship is limited to stable single-phase solid solutions in which precipitation, phase separation, grain-boundary effects, and other strengthening mechanisms do not dominate.
Minor grain-size variations and processing-induced residual stresses may confound the quantitative relationship between atomic size mismatch and hardness or strength.
Failure of increased atomic size mismatch to produce systematically increased lattice distortion, hardness, and strength would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
